frames.text: Checking that now.

Good question — and the surprising part is that the Moon isn't actually bigger near the horizon. If you measure it (even just with a photo or by holding up a pencil at arm's length), it's essentially the same size, maybe even very slightly smaller, than when it's overhead.

What's happening is a perceptual illusion called the "Moon illusion." The leading explanation is that your brain judges size relative to surrounding objects. Near the horizon, the Moon appears alongside trees, buildings, and the horizon line, giving your brain visual cues for distance and making the Moon seem farther away — and something that looks far away but still takes up the same amount of your visual field gets perceived as larger (this is related to the Ponzo illusion, where converging lines trick your brain about relative size). Up high in an empty sky, there's nothing to compare it to, so it looks smaller.

It's not caused by atmospheric magnification or refraction, despite how common that explanation sounds — the atmosphere does make the Moon look more reddish/orange near the horizon (that part IS atmospheric, from scattering), but it doesn't meaningfully change its apparent size. Interestingly, the illusion isn't fully settled science — it's one of the oldest known optical illusions (described since antiquity), and psychologists still debate the exact mechanism, but the relative-size/distance-cue explanation is the most widely accepted one.
